source.title: The Normalization Method for Alleviating Pathological Sharpness in Wide Neural Networks
source.authors: Ryo Karakida; S. Akaho; S. Amari

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports results about Fisher information matrix sharpness under normalization, but does not measure train/test error gaps or test the specific generalization measures in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper's own results concern FIM eigenvalues and gradient-descent training loss. Its statements linking sharpness to generalization cite prior work; they are not results measuring generalization in this study.
record.test_reason: The study measures FIM eigenvalues at random initialization and training-loss convergence on Gaussian teacher-generated data. It reports no held-out performance or generalization gaps, and does not test V7's magnitude-aware perturbation measure or its ranking against other measures. Generalization connections are motivation drawn from prior work.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that last-layer batch normalization, particularly mean subtraction, reduces pathological FIM sharpness when sample size scales appropriately with width. Middle-layer batch normalization and layer normalization do not generally remove it under the analyzed assumptions. Their training experiments suggest that mean subtraction permits larger learning rates for convergence; they do not demonstrate improved generalization.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes FIM eigenvalues in randomly initialized wide fully connected networks and gradient-descent training loss; it does not test the original generalization methods or outcomes.
record.method_sensitivity: The effect depends on normalization location and on the width-to-sample-size condition; the paper reports last-layer mean subtraction alleviates sharpness when T scales with M, while middle-layer batch normalization and layer normalization do not generally do so.

fits_no_version.finding: Last-layer mean subtraction greatly reduces the largest FIM eigenvalue when sample count scales with width; experiments with T = M find O(1) eigenvalues. It also permits larger learning rates for training convergence.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Last-layer mean subtraction can alleviate width-dependent FIM sharpness and improve gradient-descent trainability under the analyzed conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: Middle-layer batch normalization with nonnegative activations retains a width-proportional FIM eigenvalue lower bound. Layer normalization also retains width-proportional sharpness under the theorem's assumptions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Normalization location and type determine whether pathological FIM sharpness persists in wide randomly initialized networks.

record.problems: The study analyzes random initialization rather than trained networks' train/test gaps. The learning-rate experiment uses a single training trial in Figure 2, and the paper states that random-seed variation produces stripe patterns. The sharpness results are theoretical bounds and eigenvalue measurements, not direct measurements of generalization.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for the supplementary ten-trial training-loss figure: it reports the minimum training loss over trials, but duplicates the same normalization comparison and does not measure generalization.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting alongside natural-label held-out accuracy and chance-level random-label held-out accuracy.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Held-out image-classification performance of convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer generalization under limited or broader tuning.
Large-batch held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout's effect on held-out error across data sizes, configurations and augmentation conditions.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its correlation with train/test gaps among trained networks, and its ranking relative to norm- and margin-based measures.
Test-accuracy effects of removing memorized versus randomly selected training examples.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are evaluated against the supplied claim versions, not against the study's separate normalization hypotheses. No additional results bearing on those versions appear in the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: Memorization of random labels and generalization on natural labels.
Test error as width increases beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classification generalization.
Generalization differences among adaptive and non-adaptive optimizers.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance and its correlation with train/test gaps; the paper measures FIM eigenvalues instead.
Effect on test accuracy of removing memorized training examples.

rows.subject: DNNs with random Gaussian weights, biases, and input samples
rows.operation_detail: Measured largest FIM eigenvalue without last-layer mean subtraction.
rows.measure: Largest FIM eigenvalue (λmax); described as pathologically large without mean subtraction.
rows.value: Experimental values were much higher than with mean subtraction.
rows.uncertainty: Error bars over 100 different ensembles; exact values not stated.
rows.note: The text describes the comparison but gives no numerical eigenvalue values.
rows.check: The FIM eigenvalue comparison cannot establish any claim version; the existing state is appropriate.

rows.subject: DNNs with random Gaussian weights, biases, and input samples
rows.operation_detail: Measured largest FIM eigenvalue with mean subtraction in the last layer.
rows.measure: Largest FIM eigenvalue (λmax); authors report it became O(1) and pathological sharpness disappeared.
rows.baseline: Without mean subtraction: λmax is pathologically large; exact value not stated.
rows.value: λmax became O(1); exact value not stated.
rows.uncertainty: Error bars over 100 different ensembles; exact values not stated.
rows.note: The text reports the qualitative result and says experimental values were much lower than without mean subtraction.
rows.check: The reported O(1) eigenvalue is a normalization result, not evidence of a version's generalization effect.

rows.subject: DNNs with random Gaussian weights, biases, and input samples
rows.operation_detail: Measured largest FIM eigenvalue after batch normalization in all middle layers, leaving the last layer unnormalized.
rows.measure: Theorem gives an asymptotic lower bound of order M for λmax; authors conclude pathological sharpness remains unavoidable in many settings.
rows.uncertainty: Asymptotic bound; no error bar stated.
rows.note: The result is a theoretical lower bound, not an empirical train/test-gap measurement.
rows.check: This is a theoretical bound, not a measured generalization result. The value swaps the order parameters: the bound is α_(L−1) M [(T−1) q̂_st,BN^(L−1)/T + q̂_t,BN^(L−1)/T]. The theorem is not restricted to α_l = C = 1 and L = 3.

rows.subject: DNNs with random Gaussian weights, biases, and input samples
rows.operation_detail: Measured largest FIM eigenvalue under layer normalization.
rows.measure: Theorem bounds λmax between quantities proportional to √M and M; authors conclude layer normalization does not alleviate pathological sharpness.
rows.uncertainty: Asymptotic bounds; no error bar stated.
rows.note: This measures FIM sharpness, not a generalization gap.
rows.check: This theoretical FIM bound cannot establish any version. Both bounds are proportional to M: [αs/((C−2)η1κ′1)]M ≤ λmax ≤ √(αs)M, rather than bounding it between orders √M and M. The listed C = 1 contradicts the theorem's C > 2 condition; L = 3 and α_l = 1 are not theorem restrictions.

rows.subject: Deep ReLU networks
rows.operation_detail: Compared training losses across widths and fixed learning rates, with and without last-layer mean subtraction.
rows.measure: Training loss; losses above 10³ were classified as exploded.
rows.baseline: With last-layer mean subtraction, larger learning rates allowed convergence independently of width; exact values not stated.
rows.value: Training above the theoretical 2/λmax line exploded in sufficiently wide networks.
rows.uncertainty: Single trial with fixed initialization in Figure 2; no uncertainty reported.
rows.note: Training loss and convergence are reported, not held-out performance.
rows.check: Training-loss explosion cannot establish held-out performance as width increases. The authors explicitly identify this unnormalized experiment as a reproduction of reference [20]; preserve that attribution.

rows.subject: Deep ReLU networks
rows.operation_detail: Compared training losses across widths and fixed learning rates with last-layer mean subtraction.
rows.measure: Training loss; authors report larger learning rates allowed convergence and were independent of width.
rows.baseline: Without normalization, training above the theoretical 2/λmax line exploded in sufficiently wide networks.
rows.value: Mean subtraction allowed larger learning rates for convergence; exact values not stated.
rows.uncertainty: Single trial with fixed initialization in Figure 2; authors note random-seed stripe patterns.
rows.note: The supplementary Figure S.2 reports ten trials and the minimum training loss across trials, but this remains a training-convergence result.
rows.check: Larger learning rates permitting training convergence do not establish any claim version's generalization effect.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
